title: Beryl's Bouncy Castle Surprise
markdown:
Beryl the beaver believed a window was a promise you could see through. He was a cleaner by trade and by temperament. His days ran to quiet splashes, the long glide of a squeegee, and the particular peace of glass that had given up its smears. He found his comfort not in rustling leaves, which refused to stay numbered, but in lists: long, neat, and complete, every task and every pledge set down as if ink were a kind of dam.

His own dam was a masterpiece of angles. The woodpile stood in geometric stacks. His cleaning routes were charted like the flight of geese that had read a timetable. A promise, to Beryl, was as binding as oak roots. Order was the pattern he trusted the world to keep.

Then the school announced its summer fair.

The headmaster, a badger of considerable fluff and more considerable enthusiasm, had been praising the day for weeks. Berry pies scented the paths. Beryl, caught in the cheerful noise, heard himself say, “I shall clean all the windows.” The words were not loud. They were, for him, as final as carved stone.

Afterward came the cold arithmetic. The grounds were a sprawl of panes: tiny circles on the hamster cages, high arches on the library that seemed to scrape sky, and the slippery curve of the goldfish pond’s viewing bubble. His lists, so reliable on ordinary Tuesdays, felt like a single leaf trying to hold a river.

He hunched over his favourite ledger until his brow furrowed like a ploughed field. Grids. Tiny squares. Categories for glass that refused to be the same shape twice. The usual joy of crossing a line stayed somewhere else, lost in the size of the job.

Ivy the alpaca trotted in, her wool a weather of creams and caramels. “Beryl, my dear fellow,” she bleated, warm as a patch of sun. “You look as if you are counting dewdrops on a web. What is the matter?”

Ivy’s idea of help often arrived with unintended weather. She had been given the decorations, which meant streamers in places streamers had not applied for. Beryl explained, voice a little unsteady, the windows, the lists, the dread. Ivy, ever the dive-right-in sort, proposed the biggest panes first.

“Just begin!” she chirped, and before he could file an objection she was climbing a wobbling tower of prize-winning pumpkins to reach a high library light. The tower expressed an opinion. Beryl’s paw hovered over a new sub-list titled Pumpkin-Related Hazards. If only the headmaster had asked for a dam. Dams he understood.

A small clear voice cut through the din.

Lily stood with pigtails that had their own agenda and a sticky finger aimed at the immense bouncy castle, currently a storm of joyful children. “Mr. Beryl,” she said, “what is the point of the bouncy castle?”

He froze, squeegee in mid-air. He looked at her earnest face, then at the undulating colour, then at the list that was meant to march him from pane to pane. He understood clean glass: it let in light. He understood a good list: it brought the day to heel. The point of a castle that existed to throw people gently at the sky had never been given a heading.

For a moment he wanted a category badly enough to invent a foolish one. Then he did something his ledger had not scheduled. He watched.

Children rose and sank. Ivy, a streamer now married to one ear, laughed as if the tangle were the decoration. Popcorn, sugar, damp grass, summer. Under his paws the castle thrummed, a ridiculous heartbeat. Laughter came back off the walls like bright coins. The forest, he was beginning to suspect, did not publish its secrets all at once.

He knelt. His whiskers twitched with a new and unofficial kind of attention.

“Well, Lily,” he said, softer than reeds. “I think the point is to feel as light as a dandelion seed that has somewhere to be.”

He helped her up. They stood together while the castle went on being unfileable. The school’s windows still waited, a real job, not a riddle. Beryl looked at them and did not add a sermon to the ledger. He picked the nearest low pane of the refreshment hut, breathed on it, and cleaned that one because it was in front of him and the light wanted in. Ivy, descending from pumpkin politics with as much dignity as wool allows, held the bucket. Lily pressed her nose to the new shine and left a print he did not immediately erase.

That night, by a sensible moon, Beryl still made lists. Some things need order, as any beaver knows. He wrote the remaining windows in a calm column. At the bottom he left a square empty, not from forgetfulness, but because the castle’s thrum had refused a heading, and he had decided, for once, to let a blank do the work of a line.
characters: Beryl (quiet beaver window cleaner), Ivy (alpaca friend)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
